title: Yes, No, Please and Thank You
description: The words that make you polite before you can make a sentence — yes, no, please, thanks and their replies — plus the God-phrases every Egyptian uses whether or not they pray.
approach: GPA Phase 1 — receptive first, with short acted exchanges at a shop counter. Each particle is heard in a two-line scene before its card appears. Optional shadowing of the four replies.
unlock_condition: ≥9/12 correct on the scene quiz (hear the exchange, tap the missing word)
can_do: Say yes, no, please and thank you and answer thanks
Apologise and get someone's attention politely
Use the everyday religious phrases everyone uses

grammar.title: من فضلك، من فضلكِ — the same ending again
grammar.explanation: You met -ak and -ik on إزيك in Lesson 2. They turn up again on please and sorry: من فضلك to a man (min faḍlak), من فضلكِ to a woman (min faḍlik); لو سمحت to a man, لو سمحتي to a woman. And a woman saying sorry says آسفة, with an -a on the end, where a man says آسف. Nothing to build yet — just hear which one is used and copy it.

culture.title: God-phrases are grammar, not piety
culture.note: إن شاء الله ('God willing') goes on anything in the future — a plan, a promise, a bus arriving — and Egyptians of every religion say it. الحمد لله ('praise God') answers how-are-you, follows a meal, and greets good news. ما شاء الله is said at anything admirable — a baby, a new car, your Arabic — to ward off the evil eye; compliment without it and an Egyptian grandmother will add it for you. Use them freely: leaving them out sounds colder than putting them in.

phrases.english: Well done — God has willed it (on you)
Thank God you arrived safely (welcome back)

culture.title: معلش — the word that runs Cairo
culture.note: معلش means 'never mind', 'sorry', 'it's nothing' and 'excuse me' all at once. Bump into someone: معلش. Someone bumps into you: معلش. The waiter is late: معلش. It defuses almost anything, and hearing it with a shrug is the sound of the city forgiving itself. The reply to thanks is العفو, or the warmer ربنا يخليك ('may God keep you'), which itself is also a way of saying thank you.

phrases.english: May God keep you (thank you / you're welcome)

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Egyptian yes, and the word you will use most. نعم is for answering when someone calls your name, or on the phone — not for 'yes'. Gulf إي and Yemeni forms will not sound Egyptian.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man nodding with a thumbs-up, a clear green tick above him.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any yes answer; a nod plus أيوه is common in interviews.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Egyptian no ends in a sharp catch in the throat: laʾ, not a drawn-out laa. Often softened: لأ شكراً, or لأ معلش. A tongue-click with a small chin-lift means the same thing without a word.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman shaking her head with a raised palm, a red cross above her.
vocabulary.video_hint: A refusal at a counter or table; the head-shake or tongue-click alongside it.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Please when asking for something: to a woman من فضلكِ (min faḍlik). It shares the job with لو سمحت — Egyptians use both, and either makes a bare request polite. Note ض: a heavy d.
vocabulary.image_scene: A customer at a bakery counter pointing at a loaf with an open, polite hand.
vocabulary.video_hint: Ordering at a counter; the word is usually at the end of the request.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'if you permit'. This is how you call a waiter, stop a stranger, or get past someone — and it also means please. To a woman: لو سمحتي (law samaḥti). The single most useful politeness word in Cairo.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman raising a hand to catch a waiter's eye across a busy café.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone calling a waiter or asking a stranger; the phrase opens the exchange.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Universal Arabic and perfectly Egyptian. Warmer options you will hear: متشكر / متشكرة (mutshakkir), and ربنا يخليك. Egyptians often put a hand on the chest as they say it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man with his right hand flat on his chest, giving a small nod of thanks.
vocabulary.video_hint: Thanks at the end of any exchange; the hand-on-heart gesture is the visual cue.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The standard reply to شكراً. Also heard: عفواً, and the friendlier ولا يهمك ('don't mention it'). Say something — leaving thanks unanswered is odd.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shopkeeper waving a hand as if to say 'it's nothing', smiling.
vocabulary.video_hint: The reply to a thank-you at a counter or door.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A real apology, for when you were actually wrong. A woman says آسفة (asfa). For small bumps and delays Egyptians reach for معلش instead — آسف on its own can sound a bit heavy.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man with palms pressed together at his chest, head slightly bowed, apologetic face.
vocabulary.video_hint: An apology after a mistake; sitcom scenes are full of أنا آسف.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'walking' — 'that works'. The everyday Egyptian okay for agreeing to a plan or a price. Also طيب (well then) and تمام (perfect). Never Gulf زين.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman giving an easy okay gesture with her hand, thumb and finger in a circle.
vocabulary.video_hint: Agreement to a plan or a price; often the last word of a negotiation.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'Naturally' — the Egyptian of course, said with a little shrug. أكيد ('sure') does the same job. First contact with ط, a heavy t.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man spreading his hands with an easy 'obviously' expression.
vocabulary.video_hint: An emphatic yes to a request or invitation.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Goes on every future plan and every promise. It also does the work of a soft 'maybe' or even a polite 'no' — if a taxi driver says بكره إن شاء الله about fixing something, do not hold your breath.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man looking up with an open palm, a calendar page showing tomorrow on the wall behind.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any mention of a plan or the future; listen for it at the end of the sentence.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The answer to how-are-you, the word after a meal, the reaction to good news. Said by everyone. Alone it is a complete, polite answer.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman with her hand on her heart looking relieved, a finished plate on the table.
vocabulary.video_hint: Reply in greeting scenes; said after eating in cooking and family vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'there is no problem'. The reassuring reply to an apology or a request. ولا يهمك ('don't let it bother you') is the warmer cousin.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shopkeeper waving both hands loosely, smiling — 'it's nothing'.
vocabulary.video_hint: The reply to an apology; often paired with معلش.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said at anything admirable to admire without envy — a child, a house, a skill. Say it whenever you compliment; an unprotected compliment makes people uneasy.
vocabulary.image_scene: A grandmother admiring a baby with a wide smile, hand raised in blessing.
vocabulary.video_hint: Reactions to a baby, a car or a house; the visual is admiration.

vocabulary.english: go ahead / here you are / come in
vocabulary.teaching_note: The word for handing something over, inviting someone in, or telling them to sit or start. To a woman: اتفضلي; to a group: اتفضلوا. You will hear it a dozen times a day.
vocabulary.image_scene: A host holding a door open with an open-palm gesture toward the room inside.
vocabulary.video_hint: A host or waiter handing something over or inviting someone in.

dialogue.speaker: Baker
dialogue.arabic: مفيش مشكلة. أشوفك بكره إن شاء الله
dialogue.transliteration: mafiish mushkila. ashuufak bukra in shaaʾ allaah
dialogue.english: No problem. See you tomorrow, God willing

sound_spotlight.explanation: Both are made in the throat, but ع is a squeeze with the voice on — like the start of a groan — while ء is a clean stop, the gap in 'uh-oh'. معلش and العفو have ع; أيوه and لأ have ء. Say ع as 'a' with a tightened throat and you will be understood.
A heavy d: tongue pressed flat and pulled back, so the vowels around it darken. Heard passively here in two of the politest words in the lesson.
A heavy t, made the same way as ض but without the voice. Compare it with the plain ت in اتفضل — the ط sounds thicker.

lesson_sequence.detail: A bakery window at dusk, a queue for baladi bread. One line of English: today you learn the words that make you polite before you can make a sentence. Tap يلا.
Seven two-line exchanges acted at the counter (please/thanks/reply, sorry/no problem, yes, no, excuse me). Audio auto-plays; Arabic on screen; English small and grey.
Fifteen word cards with illustration and native audio, grouped: replies, particles, God-phrases. Tap to replay.
A scene replays with one line silenced; four cards appear; tap the word that belongs there. Distractors are from this lesson.
Three short authentic clips; the learner taps every time they hear إن شاء الله, الحمد لله or ما شاء الله. Counts shown afterwards.
The four replies — العفو, مفيش مشكلة, الحمد لله, إن شاء الله — played and echoed with a record-and-compare bar. No score.
Twelve gap-fill items, audio only. Counter rolls to 41 words. Nudge: thank someone in Arabic today and wait for the reply.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Say شكراً to an Arabic speaker today — a shopkeeper, a colleague, a friend — and listen for العفو or ربنا يخليك coming back.
real_world_prompts.context: Lesson-complete screen. One-word production with a predictable reply.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you mention a plan to an Egyptian friend, add إن شاء الله at the end and watch them relax.
real_world_prompts.context: Follow-up notification. Practises the most frequent God-phrase in its natural position.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Tell your tutor: 'Say something to me and I'll answer only with أيوه, لأ, ماشي or معلش.' Keep it going for a minute.
real_world_prompts.context: Tutor prompt. A yes/no/okay listening game that forces recognition of questions before the learner can form them.

لو سمحت من فضلك شكراً بالمصري
